steps.tx: A **developmental dysplasia** of the hip encompasses a spectrum of pathological abnormalities ranging from shallow acetabular dysplasia to irreducible complete dislocation. Risk factors are encapsulated by the classic rules: female infant (ratio six to one), first-born child, breech intrauterine presentation, oligohydramnios, and positive family history. The left hip is involved in over sixty percent of unilateral cases due to adduction against maternal sacrum.
steps.say: Developmental dysplasia of the hip ranges from mild acetabular shallowness to complete joint dislocation. Remember the classic risk factors: female infants, first-borns, breech presentation, low amniotic fluid, and positive family history. The left hip is affected in sixty percent of cases because of its intrauterine orientation against the mother sacrum.

steps.tx: In newborns under three months, clinical screening depends on two complementary provocative maneuvers: the **Barlow and Ortolani** tests. The Barlow test evaluates dislocatability: the examiner flexes the hips to ninety degrees, adducts the thighs, and applies gentle posterior pressure, eliciting a palpable clunk as an unstable femoral head exits the acetabulum. The Ortolani test evaluates reducibility: gentle abduction and anterior trochanteric elevation relocates the dislocated head.
steps.say: In infants under three months, examine hips with the Barlow and Ortolani maneuvers. Barlow tests if an in-place hip can be dislocated: adduct the hip and press backward, feeling for the head to slide out with a clunk. Ortolani tests if a dislocated hip can be reduced: gently abduct the hip and lift the trochanter forward to pop it back in.

right.title: Ortolani Maneuver (Relocates)

Palpable clunk as head slips back in

steps.tx: In infants older than three to six months, soft tissue contractures abolish the Ortolani clunk, and the classic **Galeazzi sign** becomes positive. With the child supine and both hips and knees flexed to ninety degrees with feet flat on the table, the knee on the dislocated side appears conspicuously lower due to proximal femoral migration. Restricted hip abduction under sixty degrees and asymmetrical thigh skin folds corroborate the diagnosis.
steps.say: After three months, joint tightness prevents the Ortolani clunk, and you rely on the Galeazzi sign instead. Place the child supine with feet flat and knees flexed to ninety degrees. The knee on the dislocated side sits visibly lower because the thigh bone has ridden upward. You will also find restricted abduction and asymmetrical thigh skin folds.

steps.tx: Ultrasonography according to the **Graf classification** represents the imaging gold standard in infants younger than six months, because the unossified cartilaginous femoral head is invisible on plain radiographs. Graf evaluates the bony alpha angle (normally sixty degrees or greater) and cartilage beta angle (normally fifty-five degrees or less). After four to six months, pelvic radiographs use the Hilgenreiner and Perkin lines to locate the ossification nucleus in the inferomedial quadrant.
steps.say: Under six months, the femoral head is pure cartilage, so ultrasound is mandatory. The Graf system measures the alpha angle of the bony roof, which should be sixty degrees or higher. After six months when the femoral head ossifies, use plain pelvic X-rays with Hilgenreiner and Perkin lines to ensure the head sits securely in the lower inner quadrant.

steps.tx: The cornerstone of management in infants under six months is the dynamic **Pavlik harness**. The harness maintains the hip in ninety to one hundred degrees of flexion and forty-five to sixty degrees of abduction, centering the femoral head within the acetabulum to stimulate normal roof development. Hyperabduction exceeding sixty degrees must be strictly avoided to prevent iatrogenic avascular necrosis of the femoral head caused by medial circumflex compression.
steps.say: Treat infants under six months with a Pavlik harness. This dynamic splint holds the hips flexed to ninety degrees and gently abducted to forty-five degrees, keeping the femoral head centered so the socket deepens normally. Never force abduction beyond sixty degrees, or you will pinch the medial femoral circumflex artery and cause avascular necrosis.

quiz.q: Which clinical maneuver tests for the reducibility of a dislocated hip in a newborn infant?
quiz.explain: The Ortolani test evaluates the reducibility of a dislocated hip: gentle abduction and anterior lifting of the greater trochanter relocates the femoral head with a palpable clunk.

quiz.q: What iatrogenic complication is precipitated by excessive hip hyperabduction (>60 degrees) in a Pavlik harness?
options: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head
Complete rupture of the ligamentum teres
Premature closure of the triradiate cartilage
quiz.explain: Excessive hip abduction (>60 degrees) compresses the ascending retinacular vessels of the medial femoral circumflex artery against the pelvic brim, causing iatrogenic avascular necrosis.
